title: Prototyping with AI
tagline: Go from spec to a clickable prototype outline without waiting on an engineer.
intro: You don't need to know how to code to get a prototype in front of people this week. What you need is the same PM skill from Week 2 — a structured prompt — pointed at describing screens and states instead of describing a compliance rule.

scenario.context: The I-9 Completion Assistant guardrail file from Week 3 is written. Now design and engineering need to see roughly what the HR-admin-facing tool looks like before committing real build time. (The same outline-first approach applies to any Employer Services admin tool — an Unemployment Cost Management claims-review dashboard would start from the same three questions: what does the admin see, what can they change, and what's the one moment worth testing first.)
scenario.brief: Outline a 3-screen flow for the HR admin's view of the I-9 Completion Assistant: (1) the incoming new-hire submission with the AI's flagged issues, (2) the review/edit screen where the admin resolves or overrides a flag, (3) the escalation state when a submission is routed for manual review.

sections.heading: Screen 1 — Incoming submission
sections.learning: Describe states, not just layout. 'A form with a submit button' is a layout. 'A list of flagged issues that's empty until review is complete, with each flag showing its cited requirement' is a prototype outline an AI tool can actually build something useful from.

example.text: New hire's submitted I-9 fields and document images on the left. AI's flagged issues on the right, each showing the specific field, the federal requirement it fails to meet, and a suggested next step. A summary badge at the top shows flag count, or 'No issues found' in the clear case.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 1
field.help: What does the HR admin see when a new hire's submission with AI flags first appears?
field.placeholder: Describe the layout and, importantly, its states.

sections.heading: Screen 2 — Review & resolve
sections.learning: What can the admin change, and what happens when they resolve or override a flag?

example.text: Each flag is expandable to show the exact comparison the AI made. The admin can mark a flag 'Resolved — requesting new document' or 'Overridden — confirmed correct,' with a required one-line reason on override. Overrides are logged separately from resolutions, so we can track how often the AI's flags don't hold up.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 2
field.help: What can the admin change, and what happens when they resolve or override a flag?
field.placeholder: Describe the editable states and what gets logged.

sections.heading: Screen 3 — Escalation state
sections.learning: What does the admin see for a submission that's been routed for manual review (an unrecognized document type, or a hire previously flagged in an audit)?

example.text: A banner explains why it was routed for manual review. No AI flags are shown as final — instead, the relevant federal requirement text is surfaced as reference material, and the admin works from a blank review form rather than an AI-suggested one.

field.label: Your turn: Screen 3
field.help: What does the admin see for an escalated submission?
field.placeholder: Describe what's shown, and what's deliberately not auto-filled.

sections.heading: Key interaction, in depth
sections.learning: One key interaction beats three flat screens. Pick the single most important moment — usually where the user makes a decision or the AI hands control back to a human — and describe it in more depth than everything else. That's usually the part worth testing with real people first.

example.text: The override moment (Screen 2) is the one worth testing first — it's where we learn whether admins trust the AI's citations enough to act on them without re-checking the source document themselves, or whether they're overriding out of habit rather than genuine disagreement.

sections.heading: The prompt you'd use to generate this
sections.learning: Write the actual prompt you'd type into Claude or Gemini to turn this outline into a first-pass mockup or clickable flow.

example.text: Act as a product designer. Generate a 3-screen wireframe description for an HR admin tool with these screens and states: [paste the three screens above]. Output as a numbered list of UI elements per screen, no visual design opinions yet.

field.help: Write the prompt you'd use to generate a first-pass mockup from this outline.
